claims.tx: A_1 names the constellation of first actualities that A_0's motion-time horizon licenses: rational souls, sensible objects actively exercising their sensible powers, sense-organs holding their first actuality as capacities, and a temporal-narrative manifold.
claims.fr: User-voice definition; flag implicit via 'A_1 names' formulation.

claims.tx: The transition A_1 → A_2 is the perceptual kinēsis whose terminus, A_2, is the completed perceptual act together with the residual trace it deposits.

The kinetic-roles structure inherited from A_0 holds throughout: the unmoved originator is the sensible object exercising its proper quality in actuality; the moved mover is the sense faculty receiving the sensible form without the matter; the animal via the sense-organ is that which is moved.

iCit.r: The three-factor schema's perceptual application warrants citation of the DA III.10 originating passage.

claims.tx: The A_1 → A_2 transition is the decisive hinge of the entire chain: it is here that the physical world first acquires phenomenal determinacy for the ensouled body, and here that the material conditions for phantasia and all subsequent cognitive operations are first laid down.
claims.fr: User-voice; 'decisive hinge' is an explicit interpretive characterization.

claims.tx: Three preconditions must obtain before A_1 → A_2 can commence: the sensible object actively exercising its quality, the sense-organ holding its capacity in first actuality, and the medium properly disposed to transmit the sensible form.
claims.fr: User-voice enumeration; flagged implicit via 'Three preconditions must obtain'.

claims.tx: Aristotle distinguishes between what is 'capable of being seen' and what is 'being seen': the former names the first actuality of the visible quality; the latter names the second actuality in which that quality is fully present to a perceiver.

A colored surface in a lightless room possesses the first actuality of visibility without exercising it; only when illuminated and placed within an organism's perceptual field does the quality pass from dispositional to active presence.
The sense-organ must hold its capacity in first actuality—a structured readiness inherited from the organism's developmental history.
The sense faculty at A_1 stands at the second grade of potentiality—the level of the hexis (settled disposition) that is poised for activation.
The medium must be properly disposed to transmit the sensible form; direct contact between object and organ does not produce perception in the case of the senses that perceive at a distance.

The medium's affection is sequential: the sensible quality alters the part of the medium in contact with the object, that altered part alters the next part, and so on until the alteration reaches the sense-organ.

Sound is genuinely successive—we hear the clap of thunder after we see the flash because the alteration of the air takes measurable time to traverse the medium—whereas light is transmitted instantaneously, actualizing the transparent in a single movement.
The soul at A_1 is not passive in the sense of being inert; it is receptive in the sense of being ontologically prepared.

Heidegger's analysis of Geworfenheit provides a structural parallel: Dasein does not choose its attunement to the world but finds itself always already disposed in a particular way, affected by what it encounters before any reflective act of judgment.
claims.fr: Mark the parallel as interpretive: 'Heidegger's analysis... provides a structural parallel' is already a soft flag; consider 'On the reading I am developing, ...' for greater rigor.

claims.tx: Receptivity as structured readiness rather than mere passivity holds equally for the Aristotelian sense-faculty at A_1: the organ is not a blank receptor awaiting impingement but a hylomorphically articulated capacity already poised to receive what falls within its proper range.
The fuller existential structure of Befindlichkeit (state-of-mind, finding-oneself, attunement), which articulates the recursive disclosive character of mood, is reserved for the emotion section.
Gibson's ecological approach reformulates the medium-precondition: the ambient optic array is a structured field of light that specifies the surfaces and layouts of the environment.

pCit.l: Gibson, The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception, pp. 209-210

claims.tx: The Gibsonian parallel is restricted: it holds at the level of structural affordances—the perceiver encounters an already-articulated environment, the medium's structure is part of what makes that articulation available—but it does not extend to full convergence with the Aristotelian doctrine of form-reception, since Gibson is anti-mediation whereas Aristotle's hylomorphism is a doctrine of formal mediation.
claims.fr: User-voice qualification of the Gibson-Aristotle parallel; explicit.

claims.tx: A_1 names not a single state but a constellation of preconditions, each in its proper first actuality before the transition to A_2 can commence.
The central and most controversial claim of Aristotle's perceptual theory is that the sense faculty receives the sensible form without the matter.
claims.fr: User-voice characterization 'central and most controversial' is explicit.

claims.tx: The section's task is to deploy the hylomorphic analysis as the structural basis for the dual-trace thesis developed in subsequent phases, not to adjudicate the controversy over whether the reception involves literal physiological alteration, non-material spiritual reception, or intentional structure.

A sense is what has the power of receiving into itself the sensible forms of things without the matter, in the way in which a piece of wax takes on the impress of a signet-ring without the iron or gold.

To receive the form without the matter is to undergo a change formally but not materially identical with the quality of the object; the eye, in seeing red, does not become materially red as dye stains cloth, but does take on the formal structure of redness, becoming isomorphic with the quality it perceives.
claims.fr: User-voice gloss of Aristotle's wax-signet analogy.

claims.tx: The signet-ring analogy is architecturally decisive: what passes from ring to wax is the form—the structured design of the signet—not the substrate that bears the form.
The sense and its organ are the same in fact but not in essence: the organ is a spatial magnitude, but the sensory power is a form or capacity in a magnitude rather than a magnitude itself.
The sensory power is a logos—a proportion of the contraries proper to the sense's domain—and sense is 'a sort of mean' between the extremes of the sensible qualities.
Each sense is constituted by a proportion: the eye between light and dark, the ear between high and low pitch, the tongue between sweet and bitter.

Perceptible qualities are themselves ratios of their underlying contraries; perception is the organ's taking-on of the ratio the perceptible quality instantiates: the sensory power adjusts its ratio to match the object's ratio, and this formal matching IS the perceptual act.
claims.fr: User-voice thesis; 'IS the perceptual act' is explicit.

claims.tx: If the sensible exceeds the ratio the organ can receive, the motion acts on the organ as matter rather than as sense; excess brightness destroys sight, excess loudness destroys hearing, excess heat destroys touch.
When the stimulus exceeds the organ's proportional range, the organ is affected as matter rather than as sense: the motion is real and genuine damage, but it is not perception.
claims.fr: Mark the philosophical interpretation 'is not perception' explicitly.

claims.tx: The destruction condition presupposes the hylomorphic analysis: if perception were merely material alteration, there would be no principled difference between perceiving and being damaged; the logos is what makes that difference principled.
claims.fr: User-voice; explicit 'is what makes that difference principled' framing.

claims.tx: Heidegger's reading of Aristotelian perception in BCAP radicalizes the analysis structurally: aisthēsis is itself a kritikon—'a mesotēs with the character of kritikon, of the ability-to-separate one thing from another... a being-positioned toward possible objects, which is a dynamis in the sense of kritikē'.

claims.tx: Aisthēsis is not a passive imprinting but a discriminative event: the sense faculty, in receiving the form, simultaneously exercises its critical capacity to distinguish what it has received.
Aristotle confirms the reading: the perceiving soul is said to 'make an affirmation or negation' and to pursue or avoid accordingly.
White's identification of to kritikon as the unifying capacity that connects perception, phantasia, and thought is the secondary literature's correlate of Heidegger's reading.

pCit.l: White, The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima III, 3-8, pp. 9-11

claims.tx: The hylomorphic reception of form is not a mere passive imprinting but a structurally discriminative event in which form-reception and discrimination are not two operations but one.
What persists after the perceptual act is over is not the sense faculty itself but the form the faculty has received, sustained in the organ's material substrate after the object has withdrawn.

The persistence of formal determination is the substrate on which phantasia operates; phantasia is the capacity that takes up the persisting trace and thereby makes thinking in the absence of objects possible.
Persistence does not make phantasia possible, since phantasia is itself a developed capacity of the discriminative soul; phantasia operates on persistence to make absence-presentation possible.

Frede contests a reductive reading of the persistence-character: phantasiai have 'sometimes been degraded to mere epiphenomena, the lingering after-images of sensations'—a characterization Frede rejects.

pCit.l: Frede, The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle, p. 282

claims.tx: The resonant trace is not merely a fading echo but a structured residue retaining the formal character of the original perception while being materially reconstituted in the organ's ongoing physiological activity.
claims.fr: User-voice anticipation of resonant kinēsis (canonically introduced at line 55).

claims.tx: Aristotle's account of the perceptual act turns upon a principle inherited from the analysis of motion at A_0: the activity of the mover and the activity of the moved are one and the same activity, though they differ in their being.

Motion is in the movable; it is the fulfilment of this potentiality by the action of that which has the power of causing motion; the actuality of that which has the power of causing motion is not other than the actuality of the movable, for it must be the fulfilment of both.
The mover's poiēsis and the moved's pathēsis are distinguished in account but not in substrate: 'one in substrate, different in being.'
Aristotle applies this principle directly to perception: 'the activity of the sensible object and that of the sense is one and the same activity, and yet the distinction between their being remains.'
The sensible object's exercise of its power (poiēsis) and the sense faculty's reception of the form (pathēsis) are not two events conjoined but one event under two logoi.

A man may have hearing and yet not be hearing, and that which has a sound is not always sounding; but when that which can hear is actively hearing and that which can sound is sounding, then the actual hearing and the actual sound come about at the same time.
The actual hearing and the actual sound are the same actuality under two descriptions; the sounding and the hearing arise together in a single actualization.

The formula 'one in substrate, different in being' is load-bearing across the section: introduced at the motion-level in Physics III.2-3, redeployed at DA III.2, 425b26-27 for perception, applied again at DA III.7, 431a13-14 to the coordination of perception and appetite, and reapplied in the dual-trace thesis below.

The formula's persistence across contexts reflects the chain's architectural unity: a single ontological pattern—numerical identity under plural formal descriptions—iterates across levels, each application specifying a new relation that the substrate-level unity secures.

The audit-question the chapter must answer is whether each application of the formula is genuinely warranted by the cited Aristotelian text; at the motion-level and perception-level the warrant is explicit, at the perception-appetite level Aristotle himself supplies the formulation, and at the dual-trace level the formula is deployed as a structural extension.

The unity of mover and moved in the perceptual act establishes a fundamental principle of correlation: the sensible world and the sentient organism are correlative poles of a single actualization, each requiring the other for its full reality to be disclosed.

Heidegger's existential reading: Dasein is not a static substance that subsequently enters into relations but a being constituted by its In-der-Welt-sein; the receptivity that characterizes Dasein's being-in is structured openness, not passivity.

claims.tx: Receptivity—on the existential reading no less than on the Aristotelian—is not the inertness of an isolated receptor but the structural openness of a comporting being whose mode of existence is to be already disposed toward what it can receive.
The sense organ's first actuality at A_1 instantiates structural openness at the level of perceptual capacity; Dasein's being-in-the-world generalizes the structure at the existential level.

The recursive disclosive structure through which mood conditions subsequent disclosure is reserved for the emotion section; the present analysis develops only the structural-openness point that the perceptual unity-thesis requires.

Although the reception of form without matter is the defining characteristic of perception, the reception is not a purely formal event detached from the body: perception is an enmattered alloiōsis—a qualitative alteration occurring in and through the material constitution of the sense organ.
Sensation depends on a process of movement or affection from without, for it is held to be some sort of change in quality.
The physiological changes are not mere accompaniments of perception but its material substrate; the formal reception could not occur without them.
The soul is a substance in the sense of the form of a natural body having life potentially within it; the activities of the soul, including perception, are inseparable from the body whose form it is.

Two kinds of alloiōsis must be distinguished: the first is ordinary qualitative change in which a quality is altered by the imposition of a contrary (corrupting); the second is preservative rather than corrupting—the preservation of what is potential by what is actual and like it.

claims.tx: The geometer learning geometry, the builder acquiring the art of building, the sense-organ receiving a sensible form: these are alterations that do not destroy the subject's prior state but actualize a potentiality already present as first actuality.

Perception belongs to the preservative kind: when the eye sees red, the eye is not destroyed or replaced by red—its capacity to see is actualized, and the actualization is a fulfilment of that capacity rather than its negation.
In the case of sense clearly the sensitive faculty already was potentially what the object makes it to be actually; the faculty is not affected or altered in the corruptive sense.

The wax-signet analogy clarifies the point: the wax is altered by the ring (it acquires a pattern it did not previously have) but the alteration is not the wax's corruption—the wax is preserved as wax, and the pattern is a determination of the wax rather than a substitution for it.

The same structural point governs the perceptual alloiōsis (cf. the parallel development at the level of higher-order pathē in the emotion section, where the preservative-paschein structure is deployed for the determinate emotions).
The structural register at issue is paschein (being-affected), and the perceptual alloiōsis is the perceptual instance of paschein in its preservative mode.
The full structural frame within which the perceptual paschein operates is given by Aristotle's fourfold articulation of pathos in Metaphysics Δ.21.

claims.tx: Sense 1: We call an affection a quality in respect of which a thing can be altered (white and black, sweet and bitter, heaviness and lightness).
Sense 2: The already actualized alterations.
Sense 3: Especially, injurious alterations and movements, and above all, painful injuries.
Sense 4: Experiences pleasant or painful when on a large scale are called affections.
The four senses articulate pathos as the structure of being-occurrable-to that belongs to the way of being of a finite living being.

Heidegger reads the fourfold as a 'progressive narrowing': from the most general ontological structure (alterability), through the actual occurrence of alteration (energeia of alteration), to the qualitative determination of that occurrence as harmful, to the magnitude of the harm.

claims.tx: Each of the four senses, on Aristotle's own analysis, is satisfied at the perceptual level: (1) alterability is the constitutive feature of the perceptual dynamis; (2) actual alterations are realized in the resonant aisthēma as the energeia of the aisthētikon at perceptual actualization; (3) harmful alterations are operative at the limit where excess destroys the logos; (4) magnitudes are the structural feature by which perception admits of intensity and gradation.

The fourfold and the preservative-paschein distinction are taken up at the level of higher-order pathē in the emotion section, where the structural prior commitments laid down here are deployed as the architecture of the determinate emotions; here the fourfold serves as the frame for the perceptual case alone.

claims.tx: Two consequences follow: (1) the perceptual alloiōsis is enmattered through and through; (2) the preservative character of the perceptual paschein ensures that the form received leaves a trace—the organ, having been formally altered, does not return to its pre-perceptual state when the object withdraws.
The Heideggerian counterpart anticipates the emotion section's central thesis: the pathē are the ground out of which speaking arises.
The completion of the perceptual act does not terminate the kinēsis initiated by the sensible object; it deposits a persisting impression in the ensouled body.
Even when the sensible objects are gone the sensings and imaginings continue to exist in the sense-organs.

The objects of sense-perception corresponding to each sensory organ produce sense-perception in us, and the affection due to their operation is present in the organs of sense not only when the perceptions are actualized, but even when they have departed.

That part which has been heated by something hot, heats the part next to it, and this propagates the affection onwards to the starting-point; this must happen in sense-perception, since actual perceiving is a qualitative change.

The water, having been heated, does not instantaneously return to its pre-heated state when the fire is withdrawn; the warmth persists as a residual motion in the water's material substrate—so too in perception.

Aristotle gives a name to these residual affections: even when the external object of perception has departed, the impressions it has made persist, and are themselves objects of perception. The Greek is aisthēmata.
This chapter adopts the term resonant kinēsis for the residual motion understood as a whole—the ongoing activity in the sensory apparatus that persists after the sensible object has withdrawn.

claims.tx: The coinage marks two features: first, the trace is kinēsis (a motion, not a static imprint, with the ongoing character of all Aristotelian kinēsis); second, it is resonant (it continues reverberating within the organ like sound continuing in a stilled bell, retaining the formal structure of the original motion while operating in the absence of its originating cause).
White captures the reverberating character precisely (described as a 'lingering, resonating, echoing presence of sensible forms freed from their original matter,' per footnote at White p. 498).

pCit.l: White, The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima III, 3-8, p. 498

claims.tx: The resonant kinēsis is not the same in kind as the original perceptual act; it is a continuing exercise of the same formal structure, sustained by the organ's material substrate in the original cause's absence.
A terminological distinction must be made explicit before the dual-trace thesis: the chapter operates with two related but non-synonymous terms—pathos simpliciter and resonant orexis.

claims.tx: Pathos simpliciter names the perceptual event itself in its affective aspect—the basic-valence dimension of the perceptual actualization as an event, the pleasant-or-painful that is co-given with every perceiving.

iCit.l: DA III.7, 431a8-12 (co-givenness of pleasure-pain with perception)
iCit.r: Aristotle's own claim grounds the co-givenness thesis.

claims.tx: Resonant orexis names the trace of that pathos simpliciter persisting after the object's withdrawal—the basic valence as the dispositional residue deposited by the perceptual event in the organ.
The two are related as actuality to residue: the perceptual pathos simpliciter is the event; the resonant orexis is the trace the event deposits.
The terminology is reserved this way: pathos simpliciter for events, resonant orexis for the appetitive trace within the dual-trace composite.

Von Uexküll's concept of Umwelt offers a structurally productive analogue for the resonant kinēsis's ongoing function: the Umwelt is a meaningful environment that the organism constitutes through its perceptual and effectual organs.

claims.tx: The resonant kinēsis can be understood as a modification of the organism's Umwelt: the persisting impression does not merely linger as a static trace but actively shapes the organism's subsequent encounters with its environment, determining what it notices, what it ignores, and how it responds.

Von Uexküll's framework is biological and anti-anthropocentric; the present analysis restricts the analogy to the basic-valence level, where it holds equally for rational and non-rational animals—the persisting trace shapes the perceptual world the animal inhabits, whether or not capable of higher-order operations phantasia and doxa will enable.

The extension of the Umwelt-analogy to rational-animal perception, where the soul's discriminative capacity and access to articulated doxa alter the structure of the perceptual world, requires further qualifications the present section does not undertake.

The signet-ring analogy, extended to three phases, illuminates what the resonant kinēsis adds to the hylomorphic account: (1) Potentiality—the wax is pliable, the ring held above, A_1 complete; (2) Actualization—the ring presses into the wax, this is A_2 itself; (3) Residual trace—the ring is withdrawn, the actualization proper ends, but the wax has undergone preservative alloiōsis and the impression persists.

An alteration that vanished with its cause could not ground further actualities; a completed actuality that terminated in itself could not serve as the unmoved originator of the next motion—but the resonant kinēsis persists, becoming the material upon which the phantastic motion M_2 → A_3 will operate.

claims.tx: Every perception is simultaneously a discrimination of a sensible quality and an evaluation of that quality as pleasant or painful, beneficial or harmful; accordingly, every perception deposits in the ensouled body both a formal trace and an affective trace.
The dual trace is one in substrate—a single enmattered affection in the organ—and two in being, corresponding to the perceptual and appetitive faculties' distinct ways of being.
claims.fr: User-voice; explicit application of the one-in-substrate formula.

claims.tx: The argument for the dual trace proceeds along two converging lines: the first is analytic; the second is a modus tollens.

If any order of living things has the sensory, it must also have the appetitive; whatever has a sense has the capacity for pleasure and pain and therefore has pleasant and painful objects present to it, and wherever these are present, there is desire.

Every act of sensation analytically entails affective valence: to sense at all is already to be oriented toward the pleasant and away from the painful; sensation is not a neutral registration of qualities that can then be evaluated by some further faculty—sensation is already evaluative in its very structure.

To perceive then is like bare asserting or thinking; but when the object is pleasant or painful, the soul makes a sort of affirmation or negation, and pursues or avoids the object. To feel pleasure or pain is to act with the sensitive mean towards what is good or bad as such. The faculty of appetite and avoidance are not different from one another or from the faculty of sense-perception; but their being is different.

Perception and appetite are numerically one in substrate—one faculty, one event—but they differ in being. When the object is pleasant or painful, the perceptual act is simultaneously an affirmation or negation, a pursuit or avoidance.

The residual motion that persists after the perceptual act must inherit this dual structure: the sensation that deposited the trace was itself numerically one and two in being; its pathos was formally both perceptual and appetitive—unless one can argue that the residue discards one aspect while retaining the other (which Aristotle's hylomorphism does not permit), the full pathos persists with both formal aspects intact.

The enmattered-accounts argument from DA I.1 supports the inheritance directly: the affections of soul are 'enmattered accounts' (logoi enyloi) whose definition must combine formal and material aspects—the physicist gives the material account (boiling of blood around the heart), the dialectician the formal account (desire for retaliation), and the full definition requires both.

If the residual motion is an enmattered pathos, and the pathos has two formally distinct aspects (perceptual and orectic), then the residue preserves both aspects as formal aspects of a single material substrate.

The modus tollens: if the residual motion were exhausted by its formal-epistemic aspect—if what persisted were only the resonant aisthēma—then mere retention of sensible form would suffice to originate pursuit and avoidance; but the formal content alone is motivationally inert, since Aristotle insists that bare perception is 'like bare asserting or thinking'.

A distinct operation—the hedonic-orectic valuation of the object as pleasant or painful—is required to initiate pursuit or avoidance; the source of all movement is appetitive: that which originates movement is the faculty of appetite (or farthest back, the object of that faculty, which remaining unmoved originates the movement by being apprehended in thought or imagination).

The motivational autonomy of the appetitive trace is not an ad hoc addition to the hylomorphic analysis but a structural requirement of Aristotle's own commitment to appetite as the source of animal movement.

What the resonant orexis preserves is what the chapter names the hedonic tonality of the perceptual event—the pleasant-or-painful aspect that is co-given with every perceiving and that persists as a dispositional trace after the object withdraws.

claims.tx: Hedonic tonality, on this reading, is not an add-on to perception that arrives after the perceptual event is complete but a constitutive aspect of the perceptual event itself; the resonant orexis is the persisting trace of this constitutive aspect.

What persists after perception is therefore not merely the formal structure of the perceived quality but the formal structure together with the hedonic tonality under which the quality was apprehended.

The dual-trace thesis delivers the structural payoff for the same-chain-identity claim established in §1.1: the chain runs through perception → phantasma → desire-actualization not because two parallel chains have been collapsed into one but because perception itself, in its very structure, deposits both a formal and an appetitive trace.
The basic appetitive valence is co-given with perception itself; there is no perceptual stage without a desire-component.

The perception-to-movement chain IS the actualization-of-desire chain not by stipulation but because the perceptual pathos simpliciter analytically entails the appetitive aspect that drives subsequent action.

Same-chain identity is the structural articulation of what the dual-trace thesis establishes at its core: the formal and appetitive moments of perception are one in substrate, and the chain that runs through both is one chain.
The dual trace deposited at A_2 is basic valence in its perceptual instance—the resonant orexis that preserves the pleasant-or-painful aspect of the perceptual event.

The higher-order pathē that Aristotle catalogs in the Rhetoric—anger as desire accompanied by pain for conspicuous revenge, fear as disturbance at an anticipated destructive evil, pity as pain at an apparent evil befalling one who does not deserve it—are not at issue at this stage.

claims.tx: The completed perceptual act, together with the dual residual trace it deposits, constitutes A_2—the second actuality of the perceptual chain and the ground upon which the next stage of actualization, A_3, will be built.

claims.tx: The resonant kinēsis deposited at A_2 is the material on which phantasia will operate at the next stage; the phantasma is not created ex nihilo from the sensible object's form but generated from the dual trace A_2 has left in the sensory apparatus.
Phantasia, as Aristotle defines it at DA III.3, 428b10-17, is a kinēsis arising from actual sensation and necessarily similar in character to the sensation from which it arose.

But since when one thing has been set in motion another thing may be moved by it, and imagination is held to be a movement and to be impossible without sensation, i.e. to occur in beings that are percipient and to have for its content what can be perceived, and since movement may be produced by actual sensation and that movement is necessarily similar in character to the sensation itself, this movement cannot exist apart from sensation or in creatures that do not perceive, and its possessor does and undergoes many things in virtue of it, and it is true and false.

The similarity is grounded in the resonant kinēsis: the phantasma inherits both the formal aspect (resonant aisthēma, making the image recognizable as of that object) and the affective aspect (resonant orexis, making the image matter to the perceiver) from the residual motion deposited at A_2.

claims.tx: Without the resonant aisthēma, there would be no formal structure for phantasia to preserve, recombine, or transform; without the resonant orexis, the phantasma would be a mere formal schema—a picture without significance—rather than the charged image that drives desire, aversion, and deliberation.

§1.1 foreshadowed phantasia as the temporal-narrative-synthesizing capacity through which a finite, embodied, comporting being cognizes time as a coherent narrative of past, present, and future—the capacity through which memory, present perception, and anticipation are unified into a single phenomenal manifold.

§1.2 deposits the material on which the temporal-narrative-synthesizing capacity operates; the resonant kinēsis is not yet itself a temporal-narrative manifold but the formal-and-affective residue from which such a manifold will be constructed by phantasia's synthetic activity in subsequent sections.

The chain's twofold articulation—as the actualization of desire and as the perception-to-movement chain—runs through this junction: the dual trace at A_2 is what makes the chain genuinely one (per the dual-trace defense of same-chain identity established in §F above) and what supplies phantasia with the material for its temporal-narrative synthesis.

The threshold of A_3 can now be stated: the dual trace is in place; the resonant aisthēma preserves the formal structure of the perceived quality; the resonant orexis preserves the hedonic tonality under which the quality was apprehended; the two are one in substrate and two in being, deposited as a single enmattered affection that the organ now carries.
The next section takes up the phantastic motion M_2 → A_3 through which the dual trace is taken up by phantasia and rendered as the phantasma proper.

claims.tx: Three matters bear future development and are flagged here for the reader's orientation.

First deferral: the dual-trace thesis treats the inheritance of affective valence as analytically entailed by sensation in all animals (drawing on DA II.3, 414b1-6); whether every sensory affection in every animal inherits both traces bears on the wider Aristotelian claim that appetite is the single source of all animal movement (DA III.10, 433a27-31); the question whether primitive organisms with only touch carry both traces or only the formal one merits engagement in a more extended treatment of animal locomotion, with Nussbaum on MA and Caston on phantasia in animal cognition as principal interlocutors.

claims.tx: Second deferral: the mechanism by which the medium's sequential affection translates into the unified perceptual act at A_2 is not fully articulated in DA and requires supplementary analysis from Sense and Sensibilia and De Motu Animalium; the temporally-extended transmission vs. temporally-unified perceptual experience is a genuine aporia that the corpus does not fully resolve, requiring treatment of the koinē aisthēsis analysis at DA III.1-2.

Third deferral: the dual-trace thesis distinguishes basic valence (resonant orexis, pleasant-or-painful, pursue-or-avoid) from the determinate higher-order pathē of the Rhetoric (anger, fear, pity, shame, kindness, indignation, envy, emulation); basic valence is co-constitutive with perception from A_2 onward and inherited by the phantasma at A_3; higher-order pathē arise only downstream of doxa's ratification at M_2 → M_3.

relocation_i_pathos_Metaphysics_fourfold.bridge_text_suggestion: Aristotle's Δ.21 enumeration is to be read in light of Heidegger's gloss as a 'progressive narrowing': sense (1) names the most general ontological structure (alterability simpliciter), sense (2) the actual occurrence of an alteration (its energeia), sense (3) the qualitative determination of an alteration as harmful, and sense (4) the magnitude under which a harm occurs. Heidegger gathers the four under a single thesis that pathos in its widest ontological reach names the structure by which a living being is brought into its proper actuality through its encounter with the world. (BCAP pp. 131-132). Each of these senses is satisfied at the perceptual level, with the destructive mode operative only at the limit [INTERP-FLAG: this perceptual reading of the fourfold is the chapter's central placement of the Metaphysics passage; the §1.4 emotion section deploys the same fourfold at the level of higher-order pathē, treating them as articulationally-concrete instantiations].

relocation_ii_paschein_preservation_dest.bridge_text_suggestion: The unifying ground of the perceptual-trace thesis is the distinction Aristotle draws between two senses of paschein at DA II.5, 417b2-7. In the one sense, being-affected is destruction—the extinction of one of two contraries by the other; in the other sense, being-affected is preservation—the maintenance of what is potential by the agency of what is actual and like it. Hearing a sound is a being-affected of the second sort: hearing is brought to its full being, not destroyed. The same structural point governs every perceptual alloiōsis. Heidegger emphasizes the philosophical point: not all being-affected is loss; pathos in its widest reach includes the structure by which a living being is brought into its proper actuality (BCAP p. 132). [The fourfold of Metaphysics Δ.21 articulates the broader frame within which this dual paschein operates; see immediately below.]

relocation_iii_perception_as_krisis_BCAP.bridge_text_suggestion: Heidegger reads Aristotle's explanation of aisthēsis as establishing that perception is itself 'a mesotēs with the character of kritikon, of the ability-to-separate one thing from another... a being-positioned toward possible objects, which is a dynamis in the sense of kritikē' (BCAP p. 126, treating DA B 11, 424a 4 sqq.). Perception is therefore not a passive imprinting but a discriminative event: in receiving the form, the sense faculty simultaneously exercises its critical capacity. The hylomorphic reception of form is the very same event as the soul's making 'a sort of affirmation or negation' (DA III.7, 431a8-12) — form-reception and discrimination are not two operations but one. The position-taking moment that the emotion section will develop at the higher-order pathē level is already operative here at the perceptual level: every aisthēsis is co-given as pursue-able or avoid-able, in advance of any doxastic articulation.
